title: Construction of DAG Models for Autonomous Systems
problem: Constructing optimal directed acyclic graph (DAG) task models for autonomous systems (vehicles, drones) to minimize end-to-end response time, particularly for time-triggered blended task chains.
method: Proposes representation semantics for time-triggered task chains in autonomous systems and introduces a topology optimization method that improves average end-to-end response time by 4.8x compared to Floyd algorithm with O(n²) complexity suitable for dynamic task handling.

title: BLOOM: Bit-Slice Framework for DNN Acceleration with Mixed-Precision
problem: INT4 quantization limited by outliers (high-magnitude values); existing outlier-aware compression adds complex serialization/deserialization logic that dominates execution time, reducing speedup.
method: Bit-slicing framework exploiting outlier-precision separation: outliers retain higher precision (INT8), normal values use INT4; interleaved bit-level storage exposes sparsity in high-precision components, enabling adaptive dataflow with minimal serialization overhead.

title: Efficient Lossless Compression of Scientific Floating-Point Data on CPUs and GPUs
problem: Scientific datasets are growing faster than storage and interconnect bandwidth, making data compression essential, but existing lossless compressors for floating-point data are either fast or achieve good compression ratios—rarely both simultaneously on both CPUs and GPUs.
method: The paper presents four new lossless compression algorithms specifically designed for single- and double-precision IEEE 754 floating-point data. The algorithms are fully compatible between CPUs and GPUs, enabling the same bitstream to be produced/consumed on either platform. Implementations exploit bit-level patterns in floating-point exponent and mantissa fields to achieve high compression ratios, and are tuned for SIMD/SIMT parallelism to maximize throughput on both CPU vector units and GPU streaming multiprocessors. Evaluated against 18 compressors from the literature on SDRBench scientific datasets.

title: DARIS: An Oversubscribed Spatio-Temporal Scheduler for Real-Time DNN Inference on GPUs
problem: GPUs face underutilization in DNN inference workloads due to coarse-grained scheduling that cannot exploit fine-grained spatial and temporal concurrency.
method: DARIS uses priority-based real-time scheduling combining NVIDIA MPS (Multi-Process Service) for spatial sharing and CUDA streaming for temporal partitioning. Synchronization-based staging enables zero-delay DNN migration between GPU partitions. Oversubscription mechanism analyzes GPU concurrency.

title: Robustness Verification for Checking Crash Consistency of Non-volatile Memory
problem: Programs using non-volatile memory (NVM) must explicitly flush pending stores to guarantee persistence; developers routinely miss or mis-order these flushes. Existing crash-consistency checkers are testing-based and require user guidance, leaving the correctness of NVM programs unverified in the general case.
method: The paper introduces a robustness property for NVM crash consistency and proves that checking whether a post-crash NVM state is reachable from a given pre-crash execution reduces to validity of that execution under additional ordering constraints. A search-based algorithm enumerates all partial pre-crash executions and candidate NVM states, then dispatches each reachability query to an SMT solver via symbolic encoding of the program. The approach is integrated into the DPLL(T) framework to prune the search space, and is implemented in the prototype tool PMVerify.

title: Contention-Aware Forecasting of Energy Efficiency through Sequence-Based Models in Modern Heterogeneous Processors
problem: Energy efficiency in heterogeneous processors is highly variable across core types, voltage/frequency levels, and application phases with resource contention, making static optimization ineffective. Accurate prediction of efficiency under dynamic contention scenarios is missing.
method: EffiCast leverages LSTM and Transformer sequence models trained on structured data capturing energy efficiency sensitivities across heterogeneous cores, V/f levels, application phases, and contention patterns. The models forecast future system states to enable dynamic resource management with inference latency of 1.82 ms per sequence on real processors.

title: Lookup Table-based Multiplication-free All-digital DNN Accelerator Featuring Self-Synchronous Pipeline Accumulation
problem: DNN inference requires massive matrix multiplications consuming significant power; MADDNESS approach substitutes multiplications with LUT lookups, but prior analog conversion circuits are area-inefficient and accuracy-sensitive.
method: Proposes all-digital MADDNESS-based accelerator with self-synchronous pipeline accumulator. Uses LUT-based computation instead of multipliers; self-synchronous design eliminates clock distribution complexity, improving area efficiency and PVT robustness. Post-layout simulation in 22nm CMOS demonstrates 2.5x energy efficiency and 5x area efficiency improvements.

title: Late Breaking Results: BLAST: Bisection-Free Learning Approach for Statistical Timing Characterization
problem: Statistical timing characterization of standard cells requires laborious bisection analysis to extract setup/hold constraints for sequential cells, creating computational bottlenecks in timing closure workflows.
method: BLAST extracts inherent delay for data and clock paths in sequential cells as features, then applies multi-task learning with a multi-gate mixture-of-experts (MMoE) model to exploit interdependencies between setup and hold constraints. Active learning strategy improves training efficiency by focusing on high-value samples.

title: RTL Verification for Secure Speculation Using Contract Shadow Logic
problem: Speculative execution attacks exploit microarchitectural side channels in out-of-order processors, but rigorous formal verification of hardware RTL designs against speculative security contracts has been lacking, leaving unknown vulnerabilities despite proposed mitigations.
method: Contract Shadow Logic introduces a formal RTL verification methodology that augments a processor's RTL with shadow logic encoding speculative execution contracts (defining what information a processor's speculative state may leak). The shadow logic tracks information flow through speculative pipelines at the RTL level, and model checking or equivalence checking is used to verify that no execution trace violates the contract, providing machine-checked security guarantees for the hardware design.

title: "OOPS!": Out-Of-Band Remote Power Side-Channel Attacks on Intel SGX and TDX
problem: Intel's filtering defense in MSR_IA32_MISC_PACKAGE_CTLS protects against in-band power side-channels but leaves out-of-band (OOB) management interfaces exposed, allowing energy-based attacks on confidential computing enclaves.
method: Reverse-engineer OOB communication protocols to access Package Configuration Space (PCS) energy readings outside the scope of MSR filtering. Exploit synchronization via deliberately disabled MSRs to align in-band execution with OOB measurements, enabling power side-channel extraction from SGX and TDX.

title: Cramming a Data Center into One Cabinet, a Co-Exploration of Computing and Hardware Architecture of Waferscale Chip
problem: Current wafer-scale data center architectures waste integration density due to uncoordinated resource allocation between compute and memory dies, and lack co-optimization of system area across chiplet configurations, preventing optimal performance within physical and cost constraints.
method: The paper develops a wafer-scale single-cabinet data center model with configurable on-chip memory dies and a vertically stacked hardware architecture. On this model, Titan is an automated exploration framework that establishes parameter dependencies between intra-chip (tile sizing, SRAM capacity) and inter-chip (die-to-die interconnect, stacking) design variables. Titan integrates vertical area constraints, physical limit pre-checks, and a suite of reliability prediction models to prune infeasible configurations and accelerate the design cycle.

title: PISA: Efficient Precision-Slice Framework for LLMs with Adaptive Numerical Type
problem: LLM quantization is ineffective due to outliers; mixed-precision approaches suffer from value-wise granularity and complex encoding/decoding hardware.
method: PISA splits 16-bit values into 4-bit/12-bit format, exploiting sparsity in higher-order bits. An early bird mechanism uses high-order 4-bit computation to predict result importance, enabling efficient computational skips. Integrates with systolic arrays.

title: SpecEE: Accelerating Large Language Model Inference with Speculative Early Exiting
problem: Early exiting for LLM inference is bottlenecked by the predictor, which must search over a vocabulary of ~30,000 tokens per layer and incurs up to 20% overall inference latency overhead. Existing predictors also fail to integrate with speculative decoding token trees without exponential mapping complexity.
method: SpecEE introduces a speculative-model-based paradigm that uses a small draft model to reduce the token vocabulary search space for the early-exit predictor. It redesigns the predictor to exploit inherent data variation and GPU parallelism to cut computational complexity, uses layer-wise activation frequency profiling to weight predictor deployment non-uniformly across layers, and develops a tree-aware mapping that handles the full speculative decoding token tree without exponential blowup.

title: R.I.P. Geomean Speedup Use Equal-Work (Or Equal-Time) Harmonic Mean Speedup Instead
problem: Geometric mean speedup, the dominant metric for summarizing multi-workload performance in computer architecture research, is mathematically ill-defined for speedup ratios and produces incorrect average speedup values that can lead to wrong architectural conclusions.
method: The paper derives the harmonic mean speedup from first principles under two explicit assumptions: equal-work (same total work executed on target and baseline, measuring how much faster the target finishes) and equal-time (same elapsed time, measuring how much more work is done). It demonstrates algebraically that equal-work harmonic mean correctly captures the aggregate speedup for a fixed workload mix, while the geometric mean does not. The paper further shows via concrete examples that geometric mean and harmonic mean can give opposite orderings of competing architectures.

title: Free and Fair Hardware: A Pathway to Copyright Infringement-Free Verilog Generation using LLMs
problem: Fine-tuned LLMs for hardware Verilog generation inherit copyright-protected code from training datasets, creating legal risk. Existing curated datasets lack licensing checks and scale limitations.
method: FreeSet dataset (220k files) with automated curation to guarantee fair-use licensing; Llama model (FreeV) trained via continual pre-training on this curated dataset; evaluated against a benchmark measuring copyright violation risk.

title: Optimizing windowed arithmetic for quantum attacks against RSA-2048
problem: Quantum factoring algorithms require expensive modular exponentiation circuits; windowed arithmetic trades space for time but still has high uncomputation costs in memory lookups.
method: Introduces optimizations to windowed arithmetic for quantum modular exponentiation. Key innovation is reducing uncomputation costs of memory lookups by ~50% through specialized techniques. Enables approximate 50% cost reduction for memory uncomputation in factoring, reducing overall gate count by 1.5-3.4% depending on RSA key size, with optional 16% runtime reduction at 12% qubit overhead.
